newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks, bonds surge after benign wage report.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks, bonds surge after benign wage report.

text.p: An unexpectedly benign report on fourth quarter employment costs soothed inflation jitters on Tuesday, sending U.S. Treasuries sharply higher and pushing the Dow industrials up almost 100 points in early trade.

The dollar also latched on to the Labor Department's reassuring Employment Cost Index, popping above the 121 yen level for the first time in almost four years and surging to its highest level against the German mark in more than two and a half years.

Economists said the release of the report, which showed that labor costs -- or wages and benefit costs combined -- rose by a tolerable 0.8 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996, pushed back expectations for tighter monetary policy from the Federal Reserve, spurring the broad U.S. market rally.

"The Federal Reserve is likely to remain on hold, not just at the February (Federal Open Market Committee) meeting, but through the first half of the year and perhaps a little bit longer," said Cheryl Katz, senior economist at Merrill Lynch.

Over the previous four trading sessions, bond prices had slumped, long-term yields had risen roughly 15 basis points, and the Dow had shed over 200 points, partly in anticipation of unwelcome news on the inflation front.
But after seeing the labor cost report, which rose by less than the 0.9 percent Wall Street economists had anticipated, the markets breathed a collective sigh of relief.

"Wall Street came in today prepared for the worst. When that didn't happen, you saw a market with no sellers and a lot of anxious buyers," Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co said.
Treasuries were the first to benefit, with the bellwether 30-year long bond surging well over a full point in the immediate aftermath of the report.

The dollar, which opened sharply higher after rising to a fresh 47-month high against the yen and 31-month peak against the mark overseas, cheered the bond rally and rose above 121 yen for the first time since February of 1993.
Stocks were also propelled higher at the open, with the Dow peaking just shy of a 100 point gain, then drifting off its highs to trade roughly 75 points higher at 1100 EST/1600 GMT.

Over the past year, the Employment Cost Index has become a more important indicator for the markets as a result of Fed policymakers, including Chairman Alan Greenspan, who said previously that the Fed looks closely at the report in gauging inflation.

Just last week, Greenspan warned of the risks of wage-driven inflation in his testimony to the the U.S. Senate Budget Committee, raising concern in U.S. markets that Tuesday's ECI report could prompt a tightening of credit by the central bank.
Some economists said that, regardless of Tuesday's benign report, tight U.S. labor markets should accelerate gains in wages, and possibly overall inflation, as 1997 unfolds.
But others pointed out that throughout 1996, even as the unemployment rate drifted down to almost five percent, few signs of wage-driven inflation surfaced.

According to the Labor Department's report, wages and salaries rose 3.3 percent over the full year 1996, but more modest growth of 2.0 percent in benefits costs dragged down total compensation gains to 2.9 percent.
Those represent only slight increases from 1995's well-behaved compensation growth of 2.7 percent and wages and salaries growth of 2.9 percent.

"Although wages have picked up a little bit, overall compensation, which is what matters, is rising barely steadily at three percent. I think this is pretty good news," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc.
